claim: The pial arterial vasculature of the human brain is the only blood supply to the neocortex.
source: The pial arterial vasculature of the cerebrum consists of smaller distal arteries and arterioles that cover the cerebral cortical surface, and connects the branches of the three major supplying arteries of the cerebrum—the anterior, middle, and posterior cerebral arteries—with the penetrating intracortical arterioles, which deliver blood into the cortical grey matter (Cipolla, 2009; Jones, 1970). Notably, the pial arterial vasculature is the only source of blood supply to the neocortex (Mchedlishvili and Kuridze, 1984), and its redundancies are organized in three tiers: global re-routing of blood through the circle of Willis, intermediate anastomoses between branches originating from the three major arteries, and local loops formed by pial anastomoses within the same branch (Blinder et al., 2010; Duvernoy et al., 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mchedlishvili and Kuridze, 1984.

claim: Pial arteries range in diameter from 280 to 50 μm.
source: Pial arteries range in diameter from 280 to 50 μm and connect to the smaller (<50 μm) intracortical arterioles.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Duvernoy, 1999 in the preceding context.

claim: Pial arteries with a diameter between 100 and 150 μm have a centreline velocity of 42.1 mm/s in cats.
source: Using optical imaging in cats, Kobari et al., 1984, measured blood velocities in pial arteries ranging from 20 to 200 μm diameter. For example, in pial arteries with a diameter between 100 and 150 μm, the centreline velocity was 42.1 mm/s.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kobari et al., 1984.

claim: First-order arterioles in the human retina with an average diameter of 107.9 μm have an average centreline velocity of 41.1 mm/s.
source: Similar values were obtained by Nagaoka and Yoshida, 2006, for arterioles in the human retina using laser Doppler velocimetry, where the average centreline velocity for first-order arterioles with an average diameter of 107.9 μm was 41.1 mm/s.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nagaoka and Yoshida, 2006.

claim: Mean blood velocities in small cerebral arteries in the basal ganglia range from 39–51 mm/s in humans.
source: The only study in humans measuring blood velocity in small cerebral arteries was performed by Bouvy et al., 2016, using quantitative flow MRI. They estimated mean blood velocities of 39–51 mm/s in the basal ganglia, where arterial diameters range from 175 to 668 μm (Djulejić et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bouvy et al., 2016 and Djulejić et al., 2015.

claim: The arterial transit time in healthy grey matter is estimated to be between 500 and 1500 ms.
source: The arterial transit time, which includes the transport of blood water spins from the large carotid arteries in the neck through the pial arterial vasculature and the capillaries into the tissue, is estimated to be between 500 and 1500 ms in healthy grey matter (Alsop et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alsop et al., 2015.

claim: Approximately 17% of the human cortex is covered by arteries and 11% by veins.
source: However, the segmentation provided by Duvernoy, 1999, shows that pial cerebral blood vessels are rather sparse, and only approximately 17% of the human cortex is covered by arteries and 11% by veins.
evidence: The claim is based on segmentation of data from Duvernoy, 1999, as described in the Data analysis section.

claim: Pial arteries exhibit a distinctive branching pattern where an arterial branch arises at a nearly right angle from its parent vessel.
source: Pial arteries exhibit a distinctive branching pattern on the cortical surface, in that an arterial branch arises at a nearly right angle from its parent vessel (Rowbotham and Little, 1965), usually with a significantly reduced diameter.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rowbotham and Little, 1965.

claim: TOF-MRA uses the high signal intensity caused by inflowing water protons in the blood to generate contrast.
source: In brief, TOF-MRA uses the high signal intensity caused by inflowing water protons in the blood to generate contrast, rather than an exogenous contrast agent.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TOF-MRA principles.

claim: The sentiment prevails that slower flow in small arteries should significantly diminish the TOF effect.
source: For example, while the advantage of reduced voxel size for imaging small arteries has empirically been shown numerous times (Haacke et al., 1990; Mattern et al., 2018; Von Morze et al., 2007), the sentiment prevails (Chen et al., 2018; Masaryk et al., 1989; Mut et al., 2014; Park et al., 2020; Parker et al., 1991; Wilms et al., 2001; Wright et al., 2013) that the slower flow in small arteries should significantly diminish the TOF effect (Haacke et al., 1990; Pipe, 2001), and perhaps for that reason imaging the pial arterial vasculature in vivo has received little attention.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations indicating this is a common view in the literature.

claim: This study represents the first targeted, comprehensive account of imaging pial arteries in vivo in the human brain.
source: Note that while some, particularly larger pial arterials, have undoubtedly been visualized incidentally in high-resolution images, we present here the first targeted, comprehensive account of imaging the pial arteries.
evidence: This is a claim made by the authors about the novelty of their work.

claim: For voxel sizes of 50–300 μm and blood velocities in pial arteries, blood dwell times are well below commonly used repetition times.
source: For the voxel sizes of interest here, that is, 50–300 μm, blood dwell times are, for all but the slowest flows, well below commonly used repetition times (Brown et al., 2014a; Carr and Carroll, 2012; Ladd, 2007; Von Morze et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2 showing blood dwell times and by citations to literature on typical repetition times.

claim: In a first approximation using the plug-flow model, it is not necessary to include several velocity segments for the voxel sizes of interest when considering pial arteries.
source: Thus, in a first approximation using the plug-flow model, it is not necessary to include several velocity segments for the voxel sizes of interest when considering pial arteries, as one might expect from classical treatments, and the FRE effect can be described by Equations 1–3, simplifying our characterization of FRE for these vessels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the blood dwell time analysis and the plug-flow model.

claim: Reducing the voxel size from 0.8 to 0.3 mm increases the FRE by 2900%.
source: More precisely, reducing the voxel size from 0.8, 0.5, or 0.4 mm to 0.3 mm increases the FRE by 2900%, 165%, and 85%, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Reducing the voxel size from 0.5 to 0.3 mm increases the FRE by 165%.
source: More precisely, reducing the voxel size from 0.8, 0.5, or 0.4 mm to 0.3 mm increases the FRE by 2900%, 165%, and 85%, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Reducing the voxel size from 0.4 to 0.3 mm increases the FRE by 85%.
source: More precisely, reducing the voxel size from 0.8, 0.5, or 0.4 mm to 0.3 mm increases the FRE by 2900%, 165%, and 85%, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Assuming an arterial diameter of 300 μm, the partial-volume FRE model would predict ratios of 611%, 178%, and 78% for voxel size reductions from 0.8, 0.5, and 0.4 mm to 0.3 mm.
source: Assuming an arterial diameter of 300 μm partial-volume FRE model (Introducing a partial-volume model) would predict similar ratios of 611%, 178%, and 78%.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical model presented in the paper.

claim: As long as the vessel is larger than the voxel, the relative FRE does not change with resolution.
source: However, as long as the vessel is larger than the voxel (Figure 5, blue mask), the relative FRE does not change with resolution (see also Effect of FRE definition and interaction with partial-volume model and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Reducing the voxel size from 0.8 to 0.5 mm isotropic increases the skeleton length by 44%.
source: To illustrate the gain in sensitivity to detect smaller arteries, we have estimated the relative increase of the total length of the segmented vasculature (Figure 5—figure supplement 1): reducing the voxel size from 0.8 to 0.5 mm isotropic increases the skeleton length by 44%, reducing the voxel size from 0.5 to 0.4 mm isotropic increases the skeleton length by 28%, and reducing the voxel size from 0.4 to 0.3 mm isotropic increases the skeleton length by 31%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reducing the voxel size from 0.5 to 0.4 mm isotropic increases the skeleton length by 28%.
source: To illustrate the gain in sensitivity to detect smaller arteries, we have estimated the relative increase of the total length of the segmented vasculature (Figure 5—figure supplement 1): reducing the voxel size from 0.8 to 0.5 mm isotropic increases the skeleton length by 44%, reducing the voxel size from 0.5 to 0.4 mm isotropic increases the skeleton length by 28%, and reducing the voxel size from 0.4 to 0.3 mm isotropic increases the skeleton length by 31%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reducing the voxel size from 0.4 to 0.3 mm isotropic increases the skeleton length by 31%.
source: To illustrate the gain in sensitivity to detect smaller arteries, we have estimated the relative increase of the total length of the segmented vasculature (Figure 5—figure supplement 1): reducing the voxel size from 0.8 to 0.5 mm isotropic increases the skeleton length by 44%, reducing the voxel size from 0.5 to 0.4 mm isotropic increases the skeleton length by 28%, and reducing the voxel size from 0.4 to 0.3 mm isotropic increases the skeleton length by 31%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: When imaging small pial arteries, it is primarily the voxel size, not blood delivery time, which determines whether vessels can be resolved.
source: In summary, when imaging small pial arteries, these data support the hypothesis that it is primarily the voxel size, not blood delivery time, which determines whether vessels can be resolved.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Pial arteries were imaged at 0.16 mm isotropic resolution using 7T MRI.
source: Based on these results, we then proceeded to image the pial arterial vasculature at a much higher resolution of 0.16 mm isotropic, to verify that small pial arteries can be visualized using a TOF-based contrast.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the methods and Figure 6.

claim: Numerous right-angled branches emerge from parent arteries in the pial vasculature, indicating increased sensitivity to small pial arteries.
source: Note the numerous right-angled branches emerging from the parent artery, indicating the increased sensitivity to small pial arteries, and the overall high vessel density compared with acquisitions performed at conventional resolutions (Bernier et al., 2018; Brown et al., 2014a; Chen et al., 2018; Ladd, 2007; Mattern et al., 2018; Schulz et al., 2016; Stucht et al., 2015; Von Morze et al., 2007; Wright et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual evidence in Figure 6 and comparison to cited literature.

claim: Pial arteries were imaged at 140 µm isotropic resolution using prospective motion correction at 7T.
source: To assess the benefit of even higher resolution, we acquired TOF data with an isotropic voxel size of 140 µm in a second participant using prospective motion correction (Mattern et al., 2018) to reduce motion artefacts given the even longer acquisition time and higher resolution (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the methods and Figure 7.

claim: The reduction in voxel volume by 33% from 0.16 to 0.14 mm revealed additional small branches connected to larger arteries.
source: Indeed, the reduction in voxel volume by 33% revealed additional small branches connected to larger arteries (see also Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Reducing voxel size from 0.16 to 0.14 mm isotropic increases skeleton length by 14%.
source: For this example, we found an overall increase in skeleton length of 14% (see also Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reducing voxel sizes increases FRE up to at least 0.14 mm isotropic resolution.
source: In summary, we have found that reducing voxel sizes increases FRE up to at least 0.14 mm isotropic resolution and conclude that partial-volume effects are the main contributor to FRE loss in small arteries.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 5-7.

claim: Partial-volume effects are the main contributor to FRE loss in small arteries.
source: In summary, we have found that reducing voxel sizes increases FRE up to at least 0.14 mm isotropic resolution and conclude that partial-volume effects are the main contributor to FRE loss in small arteries.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and theoretical analysis.

claim: At a delay time of 10 ms between phase encoding and echo time, the observed displacement of approximately 2 mm in some of the larger arteries corresponds to a blood velocity of 200 mm/s.
source: At a delay time of 10 ms between phase encoding and echo time, the observed displacement of approximately 2 mm in some of the larger arteries would correspond to a blood velocity of 200 mm/s, which is well within the expected range (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 8 and calculation using the vessel displacement equation.

claim: For the smallest arteries, a displacement of 1 voxel (0.4 mm) can be observed, indicative of blood velocities of 40 mm/s.
source: For the smallest arteries, a displacement of 1 voxel (0.4 mm) can be observed, indicative of blood velocities of 40 mm/s.
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figure 8.

claim: Vessel displacement can be observed in all arteries visible at this resolution, indicating high blood velocities throughout much of the pial arterial vasculature.
source: Note that the vessel displacement can be observed in all arteries visible at this resolution, indicating high blood velocities throughout much of the pial arterial vasculature.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from Figure 8.

claim: Assuming a blood velocity of 40 mm/s and a delay time of 5 ms for the high-resolution acquisitions, vessel displacements of 0.2 mm are possible, representing a shift of 1–2 voxels.
source: Thus, assuming a blood velocity of 40 mm/s (Figure 2) and a delay time of 5 ms for the high-resolution acquisitions (Figure 6), vessel displacements of 0.2 mm are possible, representing a shift of 1–2 voxels.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the vessel displacement equation and parameters from the study.

claim: Inflow in large pial veins and the superior sagittal and transverse sinuses can cause an FRE in these non-arterial vessels.
source: Inflow in large pial veins and the superior sagittal and transverse sinuses can cause an FRE in these non-arterial vessels (Figure 9, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 9.

claim: Reducing the voxel size increases the vessel contrast when imaging the pial arterial vasculature of the human brain.
source: We have outlined the theoretical components and provided empirical evidence for geometrically accurate imaging of the pial arterial vasculature of the human brain in vivo. We found that reducing the voxel size increases the vessel contrast when imaging the pial arterial vasculature of the human brain, in contrast to previous theoretical and empirical treatments of the effect of voxel size on vessel contrast (Du et al., 1993; Du et al., 1996; Venkatesan and Haacke, 1997).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and theoretical analysis presented in the paper.

claim: Slow blood flow is not the main limiting factor for high-resolution TOF imaging of pial arteries.
source: Further, we could not confirm the common assumption that slow blood flow is the main limiting factor for high-resolution TOF imaging (Chen et al., 2018; Haacke et al., 1990; Masaryk et al., 1989; Mut et al., 2014; Park et al., 2020; Parker et al., 1991; Wilms et al., 2001; Wright et al., 2013), but instead found adequate signal levels even in smallest pial arteries given sufficiently small voxels (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 7 and the theoretical analysis.

claim: FRE depends exponentially on blood delivery times.
source: Both effects are driven by non-linear relationships which might have contributed to their over- and underestimation in the literature. In short, FRE depends exponentially on blood delivery times (Figure 3), such that it decreases for longer blood delivery times, and quadratically on voxel size (Figure 4), such that it increases for smaller voxels—that is, the imaging regime of pial arteries.
evidence: The claim is supported by the theoretical analysis and Figure 3.

claim: FRE depends quadratically on voxel size.
source: Both effects are driven by non-linear relationships which might have contributed to their over- and underestimation in the literature. In short, FRE depends exponentially on blood delivery times (Figure 3), such that it decreases for longer blood delivery times, and quadratically on voxel size (Figure 4), such that it increases for smaller voxels—that is, the imaging regime of pial arteries.
evidence: The claim is supported by the theoretical analysis and Figure 4.

claim: Du et al., 1996, concluded that larger voxel size increases the absolute vessel-background contrast.
source: While this distinction may seem to be semantic, the effect of voxel volume on FRE for these two definitions is exactly opposite: Du et al., 1996, concluded that larger voxel size increases the (absolute) vessel-background contrast, whereas here we predict an increase in relative FRE for small arteries with decreasing voxel size.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Du et al., 1996.

claim: Numerous empirical observations have shown the benefit of smaller voxel sizes for visualizing and segmenting small arteries.
source: Accordingly, numerous empirical observations (Al-Kwifi et al., 2002; Bouvy et al., 2014; Haacke et al., 1990; Ladd, 2007; Mattern et al., 2018; Von Morze et al., 2007) including the data provided here (Figures 5—7) have shown the benefit of smaller voxel sizes if the aim is to visualize and segment small arteries.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and data presented in Figures 5-7.

claim: Prospective motion correction enabled the acquisition of TOF data with 0.14 mm isotropic voxel size and over 20 min acquisition time per imaging slab.
source: This has been addressed utilizing a prospective motion correction system (Mattern et al., 2018) to enable the acquisition of TOF data with 0.14 mm isotropic voxel size and over 20 min acquisition time per imaging slab.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methods used in the study.

claim: Prospective motion correction allowed for the successful correction of head motion of approximately 1 mm over the 60 min scan session.
source: This allowed for the successful correction of head motion of approximately 1 mm over the 60 min scan session, showing the potential of prospective motion correction at these very high resolutions.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of using prospective motion correction.

claim: The acquisition of TOF data with 0.16 mm isotropic voxel size in under 12 min acquisition time per slab is possible without discernible motion artefacts with experienced participants.
source: However, for the data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, no prospective motion correction was used, and we instead relied on the experienced participants who contributed to this study. We found that the acquisition of TOF data with 0.16 mm isotropic voxel size in under 12 min acquisition time per slab possible without discernible motion artefacts, although even with this nearly ideal subject behaviour approximately 1 in 4 scans still had to be discarded and repeated.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of the study.

claim: Approximately 1 in 4 scans at 0.16 mm isotropic voxel size had to be discarded and repeated due to motion artefacts.
source: We found that the acquisition of TOF data with 0.16 mm isotropic voxel size in under 12 min acquisition time per slab possible without discernible motion artefacts, although even with this nearly ideal subject behaviour approximately 1 in 4 scans still had to be discarded and repeated.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of the study.

claim: Motion correction will generally be necessary to acquire data at higher resolution than 0.16 mm isotropic.
source: Motion correction will generally be necessary to acquire data at higher resolution than that presented here.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experience with motion artefacts in the study.

claim: Imaging acceleration techniques undersample the imaging data and come at the cost of lower image SNR.
source: Alternatively, imaging acceleration techniques could be applied (Candes et al., 2006; Griswold et al., 2002; Pruessmann et al., 1999), but because these techniques undersample the imaging data, they come at the cost of lower image SNR and significant reductions in scan times might not be possible.
evidence: This is established knowledge about imaging acceleration techniques, supported by citations.

claim: Acquiring TOF data at even higher field strengths would boost SNR to partially compensate for SNR losses due to acceleration.
source: Acquiring these data at even higher field strengths would boost SNR (Edelstein et al., 1986; Pohmann et al., 2016) to partially compensate for SNR losses due to acceleration and may enable faster imaging and/or smaller voxel sizes.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about field strength and SNR, supported by citations.

claim: The limiting factor for imaging pial arteries is not the vascular physiology (slow blood flow), but rather the available image resolution.
source: In summary, when imaging the pial arterial vasculature we found that—unexpectedly—the limiting factor is not the vascular 'physiology', that is, not slow blood flow in pial arteries, but rather the currently available image resolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and theoretical analysis presented in the paper.

claim: Four healthy adult males aged 30-46 participated in the study.
source: Four healthy adults volunteered to participate in the study (four males, ages 30–46).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study participants.

claim: Experiments were conducted at 7T on a Siemens MAGNETOM whole-body scanner equipped with SC72 gradients.
source: Experiments were conducted at 7 T on a Siemens MAGNETOM whole-body scanner (Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany) equipped with SC72 gradients.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the imaging equipment used.

claim: TONE pulses were not used in the TOF acquisitions because no preferential flow direction is present in pial arteries.
source: Tilt-optimized, non-saturated excitation (TONE) pulses (Atkinson et al., 1994), which are commonly employed to obtain a homogenous image contrast (Atkinson et al., 1994; Carr and Carroll, 2012; Nägele et al., 1995), were not used; because these dedicated RF pulses are most effective when blood flow is perpendicular to the imaging slab and moving in the direction of the TONE pulse ramp, for example, in the H>>F direction. However, in the case of pial arteries, the complex branching pattern of the vasculature on the folded cortex means that no preferential flow direction is present. Thus, the optimal direction of the TONE ramp is undetermined and therefore this technique is not appropriate for imaging the mesoscopic pial arteries.
evidence: This is a methodological decision explained by the authors based on the anatomy of pial arteries.

claim: The anonymized imaging data presented in this manuscript are stored in OSF accessible via https://osf.io/nr6gc/.
source: The anonymized imaging data presented in this manuscript are stored in OSF (Center for Open Science, Inc, Charlottesville, VA) accessible via https://osf.io/nr6gc/.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data availability.
